questions.title: What a prototype is
questions.text: Which statement best defines a **prototype** in system development?

options.content: The final tested version of a system handed to the users
An early, simplified working model of a system that users try and give feedback on before the full system is built
A written list of the hardware and software the new system needs
A diagram showing how data flows between processes

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: A prototype is an early model used to get feedback. D describes a DFD; C is part of a technical specification.

questions.title: The prototyping cycle
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

The developer builds the prototype, users [[1]] it and give [[2]], and the developer [[3]] the prototype. This is repeated until the users are satisfied.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) test (2) feedback (3) refines
scheme.explanation: Build → test → feedback → refine, repeated until the users approve the prototype.

questions.title: What a prototype contains
questions.text: A developer builds a prototype of a library app. Select the **two** things the prototype is **most likely** to include.

options.content: The screens and the menu linking them
Full backup and recovery of all data
Input forms filled with example data
Protection against thousands of users at once
Complete security and encryption

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: A prototype shows the interface — screens, navigation, forms with example data. Security, backups and performance are usually left out.

questions.title: Security in a prototype
questions.text: A prototype normally includes the full security and data-backup features of the final system.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A prototype concentrates on how the system looks and behaves; security, backups and speed are usually left for the final system.

questions.title: When prototypes are built
questions.text: During which stages of the system life cycle are prototypes usually built and refined?

options.content: Analysis and design
Testing and maintenance
Implementation only
After the system has gone live

scheme.mark_scheme: A.
scheme.explanation: Prototypes are used early — during analysis and design — so requirements are agreed before coding.

questions.title: Types of prototype
questions.text: Match each type of prototype to its description.

right.text: Built quickly to clarify requirements, then discarded
Improved step by step until it becomes the final system
A rough paper sketch or wireframe of the screens

scheme.mark_scheme: Throw-away prototype – Built quickly to clarify requirements, then discarded; Evolutionary prototype – Improved step by step until it becomes the final system; Low-fidelity prototype – A rough paper sketch or wireframe of the screens. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Throw-away = discarded; evolutionary = grows into the system; low-fidelity = rough sketch.

questions.title: Throw-away prototype
questions.text: A throw-away prototype is improved version after version until it becomes the final system.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: That describes an **evolutionary** prototype. A throw-away prototype is discarded once the requirements are agreed.

questions.title: Choosing the type
questions.text: An online shop in Karaganda is launched with only a catalogue page. Every month, after customer feedback, a new version adds a basket, then payment, then delivery tracking. Which type of prototyping is this?

options.content: Throw-away prototyping
Evolutionary prototyping
Low-fidelity prototyping
Parallel running

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The prototype is kept and improved step by step until it becomes the final system — evolutionary prototyping.

questions.title: Low or high fidelity
questions.text: Tick (✓) whether each prototype is low-fidelity or high-fidelity.

prefill: Screens drawn with a pen on paper
A clickable Figma mock-up with real colours and fonts
Boxes on a whiteboard showing where fields go
An HTML page with working drop-down lists and buttons

scheme.mark_scheme: Screens drawn with a pen on paper — Low-fidelity (1); A clickable Figma mock-up with real colours and fonts — High-fidelity (1); Boxes on a whiteboard showing where fields go — Low-fidelity (1); An HTML page with working drop-down lists and buttons — High-fidelity (1)
scheme.model_answer: Screens drawn with a pen on paper — Low-fidelity; A clickable Figma mock-up with real colours and fonts — High-fidelity; Boxes on a whiteboard showing where fields go — Low-fidelity; An HTML page with working drop-down lists and buttons — High-fidelity.
scheme.explanation: Low-fidelity = rough layout; high-fidelity = looks and behaves almost like the real system.

questions.title: Fidelity
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

A [[1]]-fidelity prototype is a cheap paper sketch that shows the layout. A [[2]]-fidelity prototype looks almost like the real system. A [[3]] prototype is discarded once the requirements are agreed.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) low (2) high (3) throw-away
scheme.explanation: Low = rough; high = realistic; throw-away = discarded after requirements are clear.

questions.title: Advantages of prototyping
questions.text: Select the **two** statements that are **advantages** of using a prototype.

options.content: Missing requirements are found early
It always makes the project finish sooner, with no extra cost
Users give quick feedback on the design
Users may think the prototype is the finished system
Developers no longer need to test the final system

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Early detection of missing functionality and quick feedback are advantages. D is a disadvantage; B and E are false.

questions.title: A disadvantage
questions.text: Which of these is a **disadvantage** of using a prototype?

options.content: Users understand the new system better
Errors are found while they are cheap to fix
Building the prototype adds extra development cost and time
Users feel involved in the design

scheme.mark_scheme: C.
scheme.explanation: Prototypes cost time and money to build. The other options are advantages.

questions.title: Advantage or disadvantage
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each statement is an advantage or a disadvantage of prototyping.

prefill: Users give quick feedback on the screens
Users may think the prototype is the finished system
The prototype design can constrain the designer's ideas

scheme.mark_scheme: Users give quick feedback on the screens — Advantage (1); Users may think the prototype is the finished system — Disadvantage (1); Missing requirements are found early — Advantage (1); The prototype design can constrain the designer's ideas — Disadvantage (1)
scheme.model_answer: Users give quick feedback on the screens — Advantage; Users may think the prototype is the finished system — Disadvantage; Missing requirements are found early — Advantage; The prototype design can constrain the designer's ideas — Disadvantage.
scheme.explanation: Feedback and early detection help; false expectations and constrained ideas are drawbacks.

questions.title: Endless change requests
questions.text: Users see how easy changes to a prototype look, so they keep asking for more and more features and the project grows beyond its plan. State the name of this problem (two words).

scheme.mark_scheme: scope creep
scheme.explanation: Scope creep — the project keeps growing because users keep requesting changes.

questions.title: Why total cost can fall
questions.text: Building a prototype costs money, yet it can **reduce** the total cost of a project. Which is the best explanation?

options.content: Prototypes are always free to build with modern tools
Wrong or missing requirements are found before coding, when they are much cheaper to fix than after development
The prototype replaces the testing stage completely
Users pay for the prototype themselves

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Errors found at the design stage cost far less to fix than errors found after the system has been coded or installed.

questions.title: Point and effect
questions.text: Match each point about prototyping to its effect.

left.text: Users try the screens before coding
Users help to design the system
Each prototype version must be built and tested

right.text: Missing fields are added while changes are cheap
Users accept the final system more easily
The project needs more time and money at the start

scheme.mark_scheme: Users try the screens before coding – Missing fields are added while changes are cheap; Users help to design the system – Users accept the final system more easily; Each prototype version must be built and tested – The project needs more time and money at the start; Users keep requesting changes – The deadline slips (scope creep). One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Each advantage or disadvantage should be written with its consequence.

questions.title: Should a prototype be built?
questions.text: A clinic wants an appointment app, but the receptionists **cannot describe exactly** which screens and fields they need. What should the developer do first?

options.content: Code the whole system from the receptionists' first description
Build a quick throw-away prototype of the main screens and let the receptionists test it
Install the system directly and fix problems after it goes live
Write the user guide before talking to the receptionists

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: When requirements are unclear, a quick prototype lets users see and comment on the screens before expensive coding starts.

questions.title: User interface
questions.text: What is the **user interface** of a system?

options.content: The database tables that store the data
The part of the system the user sees and interacts with — screens, menus, buttons and forms
The network cables connecting the computers
The program code that performs the calculations

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: The user interface is everything the user sees and uses to enter data and read results.

questions.title: Navigation
questions.text: Why does a prototype of a library system include a **main menu** with *Back to menu* buttons on every screen?

options.content: To make the database smaller
So the user can reach every part of the system and always return to the start
To check that dates are valid
To print reports faster

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Navigation lets users move between screens and never get lost.

questions.title: Consistent layout
questions.text: In a good interface, buttons such as *Save* and *Cancel* are in the same place on every screen.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Consistency means users learn the layout once and do not make mistakes.

questions.title: Data and controls
questions.text: Match each field to the most suitable input control.

scheme.mark_scheme: Date of birth – Date picker; Agree to the terms – Check box; Comments (several lines) – Text area; Quantity from 1 to 10 – Number box / spinner. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: A date picker guarantees the format; check box for yes/no; text area for long text; spinner limits the range.

questions.title: Choosing controls
questions.text: Tick (✓) the most suitable input control for each field of a club registration form.

scheme.mark_scheme: Full name — Text box (1); Grade (7–12) — Drop-down list (1); Membership: Basic / Premium — Radio buttons (1); Agree to the club rules — Check box (1)
scheme.model_answer: Full name — Text box; Grade (7–12) — Drop-down list; Membership: Basic / Premium — Radio buttons; Agree to the club rules — Check box.
scheme.explanation: Free text → text box; fixed list → drop-down; one of two → radio buttons; yes/no → check box.

questions.title: Why a drop-down list
questions.text: Why is a **drop-down list** used for the field "City" on an input form?

options.content: It lets the user type any text they like
The user chooses from a fixed list, so spelling errors and invalid cities cannot be entered
It makes the form load faster
It stores the city as a number

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Choosing from a list prevents mistakes and keeps the data consistent.

questions.title: One of three
questions.text: A form asks for the payment method: **Cash, Card or Kaspi QR**. Exactly one must be chosen and all three should be visible. State the most suitable control.

scheme.mark_scheme: radio buttons
scheme.explanation: Radio buttons show all options and allow exactly one choice.

questions.title: Features of an input form
questions.text: Select the **three** features of a well-designed input form.

options.content: A label next to every field
Validation with clear error messages
Totals at the bottom of each column
Fields in a logical order
Page numbers on every page

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Labels, validation and a logical order are input-form features. Totals and page numbers belong to output forms.

questions.title: Features of an output form
questions.text: Select the **three** features of a well-designed output form (report).

options.content: A title and the date
A table with column headings
A presence check on every field
Totals or summaries
A Clear button to empty the fields

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Reports need a title, headings and totals. Validation and Clear buttons belong to input forms.

questions.title: Input or output form
questions.text: Tick (✓) whether each feature belongs to an input form or an output form.

scheme.mark_scheme: Error message "Phone must have 11 digits" — Input form (1); Total number of overdue books — Output form (1); Drop-down list of sports — Input form (1); Print and Export PDF buttons — Output form (1)
scheme.model_answer: Error message "Phone must have 11 digits" — Input form; Total number of overdue books — Output form; Drop-down list of sports — Input form; Print and Export PDF buttons — Output form.
scheme.explanation: Input forms collect and validate data; output forms present it with totals, printing and export.

questions.title: Validation on reports
questions.text: An output form (report) must validate every value it displays.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Validation happens when data is **entered** (input forms). A report shows data that is already stored.

questions.title: Form details
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Required fields on an input form are often marked with an [[1]]. When the user enters invalid data, the form shows an [[2]] message. A [[3]] picker guarantees that a date is entered in the correct format.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) asterisk (2) error (3) date
scheme.explanation: Required = asterisk; invalid data → error message; date picker for dates.

questions.title: Suit the users
questions.text: A prototype is being designed for a **touchscreen kiosk** where young children choose books. Which design is most suitable?

options.content: Small text links and keyboard shortcuts
Large buttons with pictures and very few words
A long form with many text boxes
Command-line input

scheme.mark_scheme: B.
scheme.explanation: Young children on a touchscreen need big targets, pictures and few words.

questions.title: HTML prototype of a search form
questions.text:
Complete the HTML for a prototype of a library book-search form.

```html
<form>
  <input type="text" name="title">
  <[[1]] name="genre">
    <option>Fiction</option><option>History</option>
  </select>
  <input type="[[2]]" name="available"> Available only
  <button type="[[3]]">Search</button>
</form>
```

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) select (2) checkbox (3) submit
scheme.explanation: A drop-down list is a <select>; a check box is input type="checkbox"; the Search button submits the form.

questions.title: Administrator screen
questions.text: An online store needs a prototype of the **administrator screen** for viewing and managing orders. Select the **three** components it should contain.

options.content: A table of orders with order number, customer, date, total and status
A navigation bar / menu (Orders, Products, Log out)
A customer's password shown in plain text
Named buttons such as Edit, Delete and Save
A game for customers to play while waiting

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: An admin prototype needs the order data, navigation and named buttons. Showing passwords is a security error; a game is irrelevant.

questions.title: Developing a prototype
questions.text: Match each step of developing a prototype to its order.

right.text: List the screens, data and reports needed
Design the input and output forms

scheme.mark_scheme: Step 1 – List the screens, data and reports needed; Step 2 – Sketch the navigation between screens; Step 3 – Design the input and output forms; Step 4 – Test with users and refine. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Requirements → navigation → forms → test and refine.

questions.title: Prototyping tools
questions.text: Match each tool to the best description.

right.text: Fastest and free, but cannot be clicked
Clickable navigation, but fields do not really work
Realistic look that users can click through via a shared link
Real controls; can grow into the final system

scheme.mark_scheme: Paper and pen – Fastest and free, but cannot be clicked; Slides with links – Clickable navigation, but fields do not really work; Figma – Realistic look that users can click through via a shared link; HTML / CSS – Real controls; can grow into the final system. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Fidelity rises from paper to HTML; so do time and skill needed.

questions.title: A booking app for Silk Road Travel
questions.text: **Silk Road Travel**, a tour agency in Turkistan, wants a new app so that its agents can book tours, hotels and transport for customers. The agents have never used a booking app and are unsure exactly what it should do. The developer decides to use **prototyping**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- an early / simplified (working) model of the system or part of it (1)
- used to show users how it will look / work so they can test it and give feedback before the full system is built (1)

points.criterion: Purpose: users test / give feedback before full build

scheme.model_answer: An early, simplified working model of the new system that shows the agents how it will look and work, so they can try it and give feedback before the full system is built.

parts.title: Throw-away and evolutionary
parts.text: Describe the difference between a **throw-away** prototype and an **evolutionary** prototype.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- throw-away: used to clarify / agree requirements, then discarded (1)
- evolutionary: refined step by step until it becomes the final system (1)
scheme.model_answer: A throw-away prototype is built only to agree the requirements and is then discarded; an evolutionary prototype is improved version by version until it becomes the final system.

parts.title: Suitable type
parts.text: Suggest which type of prototype is more suitable for Silk Road Travel **at the start** of the project. Justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- throw-away / low-fidelity (rapid) prototype (1)
- justification linked to the scenario: agents are unsure what they need / requirements unclear, so a quick cheap model clarifies them before coding (1)
- accept evolutionary only with a justification linked to the scenario (e.g. requirements will grow, agency wants a working app early) — max 1 for the justification
scheme.model_answer: A throw-away prototype, because the agents do not know exactly what they need; quick, cheap screens let them agree the requirements before the real app is coded.

parts.title: Advantage or disadvantage
parts.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each statement is an advantage or a disadvantage of prototyping for Silk Road Travel.

prefill: Users can try the booking screens before the app is coded
Extra time is needed to build each version
Agents may think the app is already finished
Agents feel involved and accept the app more easily

scheme.mark_scheme: Users can try the booking screens before the app is coded — Advantage (1); Extra time is needed to build each version — Disadvantage (1); Agents may think the app is already finished — Disadvantage (1); Agents feel involved and accept the app more easily — Advantage (1)
scheme.model_answer: Users can try the booking screens before the app is coded — Advantage; Extra time is needed to build each version — Disadvantage; Agents may think the app is already finished — Disadvantage; Agents feel involved and accept the app more easily — Advantage.

questions.title: Prototyping a patient system for a hospital
questions.text: A city hospital in Pavlodar is replacing its paper patient records. The IT manager suggests building a **prototype** of the new screens before the system is programmed. The hospital director is worried about the budget.

parts.title: Advantages
parts.text: Explain **two** advantages to the hospital of building a prototype first.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two advantages, each identified (1) and explained (1), e.g.:
- missing / wrong requirements found early (1) because doctors and nurses test the screens before coding (1)
- quick feedback from users (1) so the design is improved before it is built (1)
- reduced overall time / cost (1) because errors are fixed at design stage when cheap (1)
- staff feel involved / accept the system (1) so less resistance when it goes live (1)
- prototype can be used for training / user guide (1) so staff are ready earlier (1)
scheme.model_answer: Doctors and nurses can try the patient screens before the system is coded, so missing fields such as allergies are found early and added cheaply. The staff also feel involved in the design, so they are more willing to use the new system when it replaces the paper records.

parts.title: Disadvantages
parts.text: Explain **two** disadvantages of prototyping that the director might be worried about.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two disadvantages, each identified (1) and explained (1), e.g.:
- additional development cost (1) — each version must be built and tested, using budget (1)
- time-consuming (1) — the full system is delivered later (1)
- users think the prototype is the finished system (1) — they expect it to be delivered too soon / are disappointed (1)
- scope creep — staff keep requesting changes (1) so the project grows / is late / costs more (1)
- the prototype may hide complexity (security, speed) (1) so the real effort is underestimated (1)
- it can constrain the designer's ideas (1)
scheme.model_answer: Building and testing several versions of the screens costs extra money and staff time before any real system exists. Doctors may also keep asking for new features after seeing how easy changes look, so the project grows and finishes late and over budget.

parts.title: Total cost
parts.text: The IT manager says the prototype may **reduce the total cost** of the project. Explain why.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- wrong / missing requirements are found while testing the prototype, before coding (1)
- fixing them at design stage is much cheaper than changing code after development / after go-live (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff find missing or wrong requirements while testing the prototype, before the system is coded, and changing a design is far cheaper than rewriting code after the system is built.

questions.title: Membership form for the Altyn Gym
questions.text: The **Altyn Gym** wants a system for registering new members. The developer is designing a prototype of the **New member** input form. Each member chooses one of 12 trainers, a monthly or yearly membership, and whether they want a locker.

parts.title: Controls
parts.text: Tick (✓) the most suitable input control for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme: Trainer (one of 12 staff) — Drop-down list (1); Membership: Monthly / Yearly — Radio buttons (1); Wants a locker — Check box (1); Home address — Text box (1)
scheme.model_answer: Trainer (one of 12 staff) — Drop-down list; Membership: Monthly / Yearly — Radio buttons; Wants a locker — Check box; Home address — Text box.

parts.title: Drop-down list
parts.text: Explain why a drop-down list is suitable for the **Trainer** field.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the user chooses from a fixed list of the 12 trainers (1)
- so spelling mistakes / names of non-existent trainers cannot be entered / data stays consistent / saves space (1)
scheme.model_answer: The receptionist chooses from a fixed list of the 12 trainers, so a trainer's name cannot be misspelt or a trainer who does not exist entered.

parts.title: Validation
parts.text: The **Phone** field must contain exactly 11 digits. Describe how the prototype of the form should deal with a phone number that is too short.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the entry is checked (length / format check) when the user saves / leaves the field and rejected (1)
- a clear error message is shown next to the field explaining the rule, e.g. "Phone must have 11 digits" / field highlighted (1)
scheme.model_answer: A length check rejects the number when Save is pressed, and a clear message such as "Phone must have 11 digits" appears next to the highlighted field.

parts.title: Form features
parts.text: State **two other** features the developer should include on the New member form.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): clear title; label for each field; fields in a logical order; required fields marked *; hints / placeholders; Save / Submit button; Clear / Cancel button; navigation back to the menu; date picker for date of birth
scheme.model_answer: A clear title "New member" and named Save and Cancel buttons.

questions.title: An online bookshop
questions.text: **KitapHub** is an online bookshop. The developer is building prototypes of the customer screens and of the reports that the shop manager needs.

parts.title: Sales report
parts.text: The manager needs a **daily sales report** showing each book sold that day. Describe the prototype of this output form. Include the data shown and the features of the layout.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any four (1 each):
- title ("Daily sales report") and the date (1)
- table with column headings (1)
- suitable data: book title, author / ISBN, quantity, price, total per book (1)
- total sales / number of books for the day (1)
- sorted in a sensible order, e.g. by quantity sold (1)
- print / export (PDF) button or page numbers (1)

points.criterion: Table with headings and suitable data

scheme.model_answer: A heading "KitapHub — Daily sales report" with today's date; a table with columns Title, Author, Quantity, Price (₸), Total (₸), sorted by quantity sold; a line at the bottom with the total number of books and the total takings; Print and Export PDF buttons and a page number.

parts.title: Search form in HTML
parts.text: Write HTML for a prototype of the customer **book-search** form. It must have: a text box for the title, a drop-down list of genres (Fiction, History, Science), a check box "In stock only" and a **Search** button.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- text box: <input type="text"> with a label (1)
- drop-down: <select> with three <option>s Fiction, History, Science (1)
- check box: <input type="checkbox"> labelled In stock only (1)
- Search button (<button> / <input type="submit">) inside a <form> (1)
scheme.model_answer:
<form>
  <label>Title <input type="text" name="title"></label>
  <select name="genre"><option>Fiction</option><option>History</option><option>Science</option></select>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="stock"> In stock only</label>
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

parts.title: Navigation
parts.text: Explain why every screen of the prototype should have the same navigation bar.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the user can reach every part of the shop / return to the home page from any screen (1)
- consistency — users learn the layout once, so it is easier to use / fewer mistakes / users do not get lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: With the same navigation bar on every screen, customers can always get to any part of the shop or back home, and because it never moves they learn it once and do not get lost.

summary: What a prototype is and where it fits in the system life cycle, throw-away and evolutionary, low- and high-fidelity prototypes, the advantages and disadvantages of prototyping, and how to develop a prototype of the interface, input forms and output forms of a new system.

blocks.content: An **early, simplified working model** of a new system (or part of it) that shows **how it will look and behave** — its screens, menus, input forms and reports — so that users can **try it and give feedback** before the full system is built.
A way of developing a system in which a prototype is **built, tested by users and refined in repeated cycles** until the users agree that it meets their requirements.

A prototype usually has the full **interface** but only part of the **functionality**: buttons may not save data yet, searches may return example records, and calculations may use fixed values. Its job is to answer the question *"Is this what you need?"* while changes are still cheap.

items.title: What a prototype usually includes
items.content:
- The **screens** and the **navigation** between them (menus, buttons, links).
- **Input forms** with their fields, labels and controls.
- **Output forms** — reports, receipts, on-screen lists — filled with example data.
- A few **key functions** that users most want to see working.

items.title: What it usually leaves out
items.content:
- Full **data storage** (the database may be missing or contain test data only).
- **Security**, backups and error handling.
- **Speed** and the ability to handle many users at once.
- Rare cases and less important functions.

blocks.title: A prototype for a clinic appointment app
blocks.content:
A clinic in Shymkent wants an app for booking doctor appointments. The receptionists are not sure what they need.
- The developer draws **three screens** in a design tool: *Choose a doctor*, *Choose a time*, *Confirm booking*.
- Receptionists click through them with example data. They ask for a **phone-number field** and a list of **free times only**.
- The developer adds both and shows the prototype again; this time it is approved.
- Only now is the database built and the real booking code written — the missing phone field was found **before** any code had to be rewritten.
A prototype built **quickly and cheaply** only to **find out and agree the requirements**. When the requirements are clear it is **discarded** and the real system is built from scratch.
A prototype that is **improved step by step**, version after version, until it **becomes the final system**. Each version adds functions based on user feedback.

Slower — each version must be well built

Requirements are **partly known** and will grow

blocks.content: A **low-fidelity** prototype is a rough model — paper sketches or simple wireframes — that shows layout but not real appearance. A **high-fidelity** prototype looks and behaves **almost like the real system** — real colours, fonts, clickable buttons, example data.

blocks.title: Low-fidelity and high-fidelity
rows: Paper and pen, whiteboard, simple wireframe tool
Figma, PowerPoint with links, HTML / CSS, a form designer
Layout, which fields and buttons exist
Real look, colours, navigation, example data
Early ideas, many options compared quickly
Final approval of the design, user testing
**How** it looks and feels to use

blocks.content:
- Saying every prototype becomes the final system — only an **evolutionary** prototype does.
- Mixing up "throw-away" with "failed": a throw-away prototype has **done its job** when the requirements are agreed.
- Thinking a prototype must be a program — a set of **paper screens** is also a prototype.

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- **Users see and try** the system early, so **missing or wrong requirements** are found quickly (easy detection of missing functionality).
- **Quick feedback** from users improves the design.
- Users and developers **understand the system better**; fewer misunderstandings.
- Errors are found **early**, when they are **cheaper** to fix → **reduced time and costs** overall.
- Users feel **involved**, so they **accept** the final system more easily.
- The prototype can be used for **training** and for writing the **user guide**.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- Building prototypes adds **additional development cost** and is **time-consuming**.
- Users may think the prototype **is the finished system** and expect it to be delivered too soon.
- Users may keep asking for **changes** (scope creep), so the project grows and is late.
- The prototype design can **constrain the designer's ideas** — later, better solutions are ignored.
- A prototype may **hide the real complexity** (security, speed, data storage) of the system.
- Quick prototype code may be **poorly structured** if it is kept (evolutionary).

blocks.title: Should a prototype be built? — weighing it up for a scenario
blocks.content:
**Scenario:** a bakery chain in Almaty wants an app for ordering birthday cakes. The managers have never used an ordering app and cannot describe what the order form needs.

- **For a prototype:** the requirements are **unclear**, so a quick throw-away prototype of the order form lets managers point at what is missing (cake size, message on the cake, delivery time) before coding starts.
- **Against:** it adds **cost and time** at the start; managers may ask for many extra features.
- **Conclusion:** build a cheap **low-fidelity** prototype of the order form and the confirmation screen; agree a list of changes in advance to limit scope creep. The benefit (correct requirements) is bigger than the extra cost.

Give a **specific** effect, not a vague word: not "it is good" or "it is expensive", but "*users can test the input form early, so missing fields are added before the system is coded*". For "explain" questions write the point **and** its consequence.

- Writing "it saves time" with no reason — say **why**: errors are found early, before code is written.
- Giving the same point twice in different words (e.g. "quick feedback" and "users comment quickly").
- Forgetting that the extra cost of the prototype is a **disadvantage** even though it may reduce the **total** cost.

theory.title: Exam practice: prototypes and their advantages

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term prototype. [2]**
An early / simplified working model of a new system or part of it (1) used to show users how it will look and work so that they can test it and give feedback (before the full system is built) (1).

**Q: Describe the difference between a throw-away prototype and an evolutionary prototype. [2]**
A throw-away prototype is used only to agree the requirements and is then discarded (1); an evolutionary prototype is refined step by step until it becomes the final system (1).

**Q: Give two advantages of using a prototype when developing a new system. [2]**
Any two: missing functionality / requirements are found early (1); quick feedback from users (1); users and developers understand the system better (1); errors fixed early so time and cost are reduced (1); users feel involved and accept the system (1).

**Q: Write one disadvantage of using a prototype. [1]**
Additional development cost / it is time-consuming / users may think it is the finished system / users keep requesting changes / it can constrain the designer's ideas (1).

**Q: A prototype costs money to build, yet it can reduce the total cost of a project. Explain why. [2]**
Users find missing or wrong requirements while testing the prototype, before the system is coded (1); fixing errors at the design stage is much cheaper than rewriting code after development or implementation (1).

**Q: Explain why a throw-away prototype is suitable for a school that cannot describe exactly what it wants from a new timetable app. [2]**
The requirements are unclear, so a quick, cheap model lets staff see and comment on the screens (1); it can be discarded once the requirements are agreed, so no poorly built code is kept (1).

- A definition that says only "a model of the system" — add **why**: users test it and give feedback.
- Calling the prototype "the first version of the final system" for **every** type.
- Listing advantages without the consequence when the command word is **explain**.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define a prototype and describe the four steps of the prototyping cycle.
Say what a prototype usually includes and what it usually leaves out.
Compare throw-away and evolutionary prototypes (purpose, what happens to them, code quality).
Give three advantages and three disadvantages of prototyping, each with its effect.
Decide, for a given scenario, whether a prototype should be built, and justify the answer.

blocks.content: The part of a system that the **user sees and interacts with** — screens, menus, buttons, forms and messages — through which data is entered and results are shown.
The way the user **moves between the screens** of a system — a main menu, navigation bar, buttons and links such as *Back* and *Home*.

items.title: Principles of a good interface
items.content:
- **Consistent** layout, colours, fonts and button positions on every screen.
- Clear **headings** so the user always knows which screen they are on.
- A **main menu** or navigation bar that reaches every part of the system; *Back* / *Home* buttons.
- **Simple language** and icons the users understand.
- **Help** messages, tooltips and clear error messages.

items.title: Suit the interface to the users
items.content:
- **Young children:** large buttons, pictures, few words.
- **Touchscreen kiosk:** big targets, few steps, no typing if possible.
- **Experienced staff:** keyboard shortcuts, many fields on one screen.
- **Users with poor eyesight:** large text, high contrast.
- Languages: Kazakh / Russian / English switch if users need it.

items.title: Features of a good input form
items.content:
- A clear **title** and **instructions**.
- Fields in a **logical order** (as on the paper form).
- A **label** next to every field; hints / examples in placeholders.
- Suitable **controls** (drop-down, radio buttons, check box, date picker).
- **Validation** with clear **error messages**; required fields marked *.
- **Buttons**: Save / Submit, Clear, Cancel; navigation back to the menu.

items.title: Features of a good output form
items.content:
- A clear **title**, the **date** and **page numbers**.
- Data in a **table** with **column headings**; sensible **sort order**.
- **Totals**, counts or averages where needed; charts if they help.
- Only the information the user **needs** — no clutter.
- Can be **printed** or **exported** (PDF, spreadsheet).

blocks.content:
- Drawing a form with fields but **no labels**, or labels with no fields.
- Choosing a **text box** where a drop-down list or radio buttons would prevent errors.
- Forgetting the **buttons** (Save, Cancel) and the **navigation**.
- An output form with **no title or column headings**, or one that shows every field of the database.

blocks.title: How to develop a prototype for a scenario
items: List the **requirements**: which screens, which data must be entered, which reports are needed.
Sketch the **navigation** — main menu → screens → sub-screens.
For each **input form**, list the fields, choose a **control** for each and add **validation**.
For each **output form**, choose the layout — table with headings, totals, sort order.
Build the prototype: paper, slides with links, Figma, HTML, or a form designer in the programming tool.
**Test** it with users, collect **feedback**, and **refine** it until it is approved.

blocks.title: Worked example — a prototype for a school canteen pre-order system
blocks.content:
**Scenario:** pupils will order lunch online before 10:00; the canteen manager needs a list of orders to prepare.

**Step 1 — requirements.** Screens: *Log in*, *Menu of the day*, *Order form*, *Order confirmation*; report: *Today's orders* for the manager.

**Step 2 — navigation.** Log in → Main menu (Order lunch · My orders · Log out). Manager: Main menu → Today's orders.

**Step 3 — input form (Order form).**

| Field | Control | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| Pupil ID | Filled in automatically after log-in | — |
| Dish | Drop-down list of today's dishes | Presence check |
| Portion | Radio buttons: Small / Normal | One must be chosen |
| Extra drink | Check box | — |
| Collection time | Drop-down: 12:30 / 13:15 / 14:00 | Presence check |

Buttons: **Place order**, **Cancel**. Error message if the time is after 10:00: "Orders close at 10:00".

**Step 4 — output form (Today's orders).** Title and date; table *Class · Pupil · Dish · Portion · Time*, sorted by collection time; **total portions of each dish** at the bottom; *Print* button.

**Step 5 — test.** The manager tries it and asks for a **count per class**; the cook asks for **allergies** on the order form. Both are added in version 2 before any database code is written.

blocks.title: Exam-style marking — "Draw the prototype of the administrator mode of an online store" [4]
blocks.content: An **order table** with suitable attributes (order no., customer, date, total, status) (1); a **main menu / navigation bar** (1); at least **two named buttons** — Add / Edit / Delete / Save (2).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State three features of a well-designed input form. [3]**
Any three: clear title (1); a label for each field (1); fields in a logical order (1); suitable controls such as drop-down lists (1); validation with error messages (1); required fields marked (1); Save / Cancel buttons (1).

**Q: Explain why a drop-down list is used for the field "City" on an input form. [2]**
The user chooses from a fixed list of cities (1), so spelling mistakes / invalid cities cannot be entered and the data is consistent (1).

**Q: Suggest a suitable control for "Payment method: Cash / Card / Kaspi QR" and justify it. [2]**
Radio buttons (1) — there are only a few options and exactly one must be chosen; all options are visible (1).

**Q: State two features of a well-designed output form (report). [2]**
Any two: title and date (1); table with column headings (1); totals / summaries (1); only the data the user needs (1); print / export option (1); page numbers (1).

**Q: A gym is developing a membership system. Describe the prototype of the "New member" input form. [4]**
Title "New member" (1); fields with labels: name, date of birth, phone, membership type (1); suitable controls — date picker for date of birth, radio buttons for membership type (1); Save and Cancel buttons / validation with an error message (1).

- Listing fields that the scenario **did not ask for** while missing the ones it did.
- Writing "a nice design" or "colourful" — name a **feature** (labels, validation, drop-down list).
- Mixing up input and output forms: reports do not need validation; input forms do not need totals.
- Forgetting to **justify** a control: say what error it prevents.
